title: Tracheostomy Obstruction: Sudden Distress Means Airway First
bottomLine: Sudden respiratory distress, inability to pass suction, absent airflow, cyanosis, or rapidly falling oxygenation can signal tracheostomy obstruction. Treat this as an airway emergency and escalate immediately.
recognize: Thick secretions, mucus plugs, blood, tube kinking, or inner-cannula blockage can obstruct airflow.
priorities: Assess airway patency and breathing, summon trained airway help, and follow the facility tracheostomy-emergency algorithm.
assessMonitor: Monitor breath sounds, airflow, work of breathing, oxygenation, secretions, and ability to pass the prescribed suction catheter.
interventions: Use authorized suction/inner-cannula management and emergency airway support per competency and protocol.
medicationSafety: Bronchodilators do not correct a mechanically blocked tracheostomy.
teaching: Home caregivers should know the emergency plan and keep required spare equipment immediately available.
delegationScope: Emergency tracheostomy care requires trained personnel; PN/LVN responsibilities depend on competency and facility/state policy.
examTrap: Treating new wheezing first while ignoring a blocked artificial airway.
oneLinePearl: No airflow through a trach is an airway emergency.

title: Accidental Decannulation: Protect Oxygenation and Do Not Force Replacement
bottomLine: An accidentally displaced tracheostomy can rapidly compromise ventilation. Call trained airway support, maintain oxygenation, and follow the emergency replacement algorithm; never blindly force a tube into an immature tract.
recognize: Changed tube position, exposed flange distance, respiratory distress, loss of delivered oxygen, or obvious tube displacement are cues.
priorities: Support breathing and summon airway expertise immediately.
assessMonitor: Assess stoma age/maturity if known, airflow, work of breathing, oxygenation, and visible tube position.
interventions: Use facility emergency equipment and replacement steps only within competency; protect the airway while expert help arrives.
medicationSafety: Sedatives can worsen an unstable airway and should not delay airway management.
teaching: Home emergency kits should include the prescribed spare tracheostomy equipment and caregiver instructions.
delegationScope: Tube reinsertion is role-, competency-, and stoma-age dependent; do not exceed local protocol.
examTrap: Blindly reinserting a displaced fresh tracheostomy without trained airway support.
oneLinePearl: Dislodged fresh trach: oxygenate, escalate, do not force.

title: Tracheostomy Suctioning: Suction for Cues, Not by Habit
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Suctioning should respond to retained-secretions cues and use the prescribed sterile/aseptic technique for the setting. Excessive or deep suctioning can cause hypoxemia, trauma, bleeding, and vagal responses.
recognize: Coarse breath sounds, visible secretions, ineffective cough, rising work of breathing, or falling oxygenation can indicate suction need.
priorities: Assess need first, prepare oxygenation/emergency support, and use the correct catheter/depth/technique for the patient.
assessMonitor: Monitor oxygenation, heart rate, secretion amount/character, bleeding, and response.
interventions: Use single-use sterile open-suction equipment when required and avoid unnecessary deep suctioning.
medicationSafety: Do not instill medications or routine saline into the airway unless specifically ordered/indicated by protocol.
teaching: Home suction technique should follow the exact training plan and equipment instructions.
delegationScope: Suctioning requires competency validation; PN/LVN authority varies by setting.
examTrap: Deep-suctioning repeatedly despite no secretion cue.
oneLinePearl: Suction the patient, not the clock.

title: Tracheostomy Humidification: Dry Airways Plug Faster
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: A tracheostomy bypasses upper-airway humidification. Thick, crusted secretions and recurrent plugging risk require attention to prescribed humidification, hydration, and secretion management.
recognize: Tenacious secretions, dry mucosa, crusting, increased suction need, or reduced airflow suggest inadequate humidification.
priorities: Verify the ordered humidification system is functioning and assess hydration/secretions.
assessMonitor: Track secretion thickness, suction frequency, airway sounds, humidification-device function, and fluid status.
interventions: Maintain prescribed humidification and hydration strategy; escalate recurrent plugging.
medicationSafety: Mucolytic or nebulized therapy requires patient-specific orders and monitoring.
teaching: Teach caregivers how to recognize inadequate humidification and device failure.
delegationScope: Routine humidification checks may be shared with trained staff; airway deterioration requires licensed escalation.
examTrap: Reducing humidification because secretions seem inconvenient.
oneLinePearl: A dry trach airway is a plugging risk.

title: Tracheostomy Cuff Safety: Pressure, Aspiration, and Communication
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Cuff inflation status affects ventilation, secretion leakage, swallowing, and speech. Follow the prescribed cuff plan; overinflation can injure the trachea and underinflation can impair ventilation or increase leakage depending on the clinical situation.
recognize: Air leak, poor ventilator volumes, new voice change, swallowing difficulty, or cuff-related discomfort require assessment.
priorities: Verify the ordered cuff status and escalate unexplained leaks or ventilation problems.
assessMonitor: Monitor respiratory status, ventilator parameters when applicable, swallowing/aspiration cues, and cuff-related discomfort.
interventions: Cuff measurement/adjustment should follow trained respiratory/airway protocol.
medicationSafety: Do not use sedatives to mask cuff-related distress.
teaching: Patients/caregivers should not independently inflate or deflate cuffs outside the prescribed plan.
delegationScope: Cuff management is competency- and policy-dependent.
examTrap: Adding more cuff air automatically for every leak.
oneLinePearl: A cuff leak needs assessment, not reflex inflation.

title: Tracheostomy Stoma Infection: Secretions Do Not Make Infection Normal
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Moisture and secretions can irritate a tracheostomy site, but spreading erythema, purulence, worsening pain, fever, or tissue breakdown requires infection assessment.
recognize: Localized moisture-associated irritation differs from expanding erythema, purulent drainage, fever, or systemic illness.
priorities: Inspect the site, protect skin, maintain prescribed aseptic care, and escalate suspected infection.
assessMonitor: Trend stoma appearance, secretions, odor, pain, temperature, and respiratory status.
interventions: Use manufacturer/facility-approved cleaning and dressing technique; avoid improvised reprocessing.
medicationSafety: Topical/systemic antimicrobials require clinical indication rather than routine prophylaxis.
teaching: Home caregivers should follow the exact cleaning/reprocessing instructions for their tube and supplies.
delegationScope: Routine site care may be delegated to trained staff; infection assessment requires licensed judgment.
examTrap: Calling purulent drainage normal because tracheostomies have secretions.
oneLinePearl: Moist is expected; spreading infection is not.

title: Tracheostomy Bleeding: Small Sentinel Bleeds Can Matter
bottomLine: Minor blood-streaking after suction trauma may occur, but brisk, recurrent, unexplained, or pulsatile tracheostomy bleeding can precede catastrophic hemorrhage and requires immediate escalation.
recognize: New brisk peristomal or airway bleeding, hemodynamic change, or recurrent sentinel bleeding is high risk.
priorities: Call emergency airway/surgical help and protect oxygenation.
assessMonitor: Monitor bleeding amount, airway patency, oxygenation, HR/BP, and recent suction/tube manipulation.
interventions: Follow the emergency hemorrhage protocol; avoid blind manipulation that worsens bleeding.
medicationSafety: Review anticoagulant/antiplatelet exposure but do not delay emergency response.
teaching: Home patients should seek emergency care for significant or recurrent unexplained tracheostomy bleeding.
delegationScope: This is an emergency escalation problem, not a routine delegated task.
examTrap: Reassuring the patient after a significant sentinel bleed because bleeding stopped.
oneLinePearl: Brisk trach bleeding is never routine.

title: Speaking Valve Safety: Exhalation Path Must Be Open
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: A one-way speaking valve requires an adequate exhalation path around the tracheostomy tube and prescribed cuff status. New distress after valve placement requires immediate removal and reassessment.
recognize: Dyspnea, back-pressure, anxiety, desaturation, inability to exhale, or stridor after valve use are danger cues.
priorities: Verify the valve plan, cuff status, airway patency, and tolerance.
assessMonitor: Monitor breathing effort, oxygenation, voice, secretions, and swallowing tolerance.
interventions: Remove the valve immediately if respiratory distress develops and escalate.
medicationSafety: Sedation should not be used to force tolerance of an unsafe valve setup.
teaching: Use the valve only according to the prescribed speech/airway plan.
delegationScope: Valve application/tolerance monitoring requires training and interdisciplinary guidance.
examTrap: Leaving a speaking valve in place despite increasing distress.
oneLinePearl: A speaking valve must leave a path for exhalation.

title: Tracheostomy and Swallowing: Cough, Voice, and Secretions Matter
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Patients with tracheostomies may have dysphagia and aspiration risk. Coughing with intake, wet voice, food-colored secretions, recurrent pneumonia, or increased respiratory effort requires swallow-safety escalation.
recognize: Silent aspiration is possible, so absence of cough does not prove safety.
priorities: Follow the prescribed diet/swallow plan and stop oral intake when acute aspiration signs occur until reviewed.
assessMonitor: Monitor voice, cough, secretions, oxygenation, meal tolerance, and chest symptoms.
interventions: Use positioning and swallowing strategies prescribed by speech-language pathology.
medicationSafety: Medication route/formulation may need adjustment when swallowing is unsafe; do not crush indiscriminately.
delegationScope: Feeding assistance may be assigned only with a clear swallow plan and report-back criteria.
examTrap: Assuming a tracheostomy protects the lungs from aspiration.
oneLinePearl: A trach does not eliminate aspiration risk.

title: Home Tracheostomy Emergency Readiness: Equipment Must Travel With the Patient
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
bottomLine: Home tracheostomy safety depends on trained caregivers, a current emergency plan, working suction/oxygen equipment as prescribed, and immediately available spare tracheostomy supplies.
recognize: Missing spare tubes, dead suction equipment, absent power-backup planning, or untrained caregivers create preventable emergency risk.
priorities: Verify emergency equipment, backup power/transport plans, caregiver competency, and emergency contacts before discharge or travel.
assessMonitor: Check equipment function, supply availability, emergency kit contents, and caregiver teach-back.
interventions: Reinforce the written emergency algorithm and transport precautions.
medicationSafety: Emergency medications and oxygen should be used only according to the prescribed plan.
teaching: Emergency equipment should accompany the patient, not stay at home during travel.
delegationScope: Discharge competency verification requires licensed/interdisciplinary oversight.
examTrap: Discharging a tracheostomy-dependent patient because routine care is understood despite no emergency plan.
oneLinePearl: Routine trach care is not enough—emergency readiness is part of discharge safety.
